introduction: Study graph representations, breadth-first search and depth-first search. Start with graph notation, then compare how queues and stacks guide exploration.

units.label: Topic 01
units.title: Think in graphs
units.summary: Describe a network, then choose a representation that fits the questions you need to answer.

objectives.text: Choose a graph representation for a sparse network.

blocks.title: A small language for connections
paragraphs: A graph describes relationships. A vertex represents an object. An edge represents a connection between two objects.
In an undirected graph, the connection works in both directions. A simple graph has no self-loops or repeated edges.

blocks.title: Count each edge twice
blocks.plain: The sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges.

symbols.meaning: The set of vertices.
The set of edges.
The number of edges incident to vertex \(v\).

blocks.conditions: For a simple undirected graph. Six edges contribute twelve to the total degree.

blocks.title: Choose the representation
rows: How do I test one edge?
blocks.caption: Common trade-offs for a graph with \(|V|\) vertices and \(|E|\) edges.

blocks.title: Read a connection matrix
blocks.plain: For the small path A–B–C, a 1 records an edge. Squaring the matrix counts walks with exactly two edges.

symbols.meaning: The adjacency matrix; rows and columns follow A, B, C.
The number of two-edge walks from vertex \(i\) to vertex \(j\).

blocks.conditions: A walk may repeat a vertex. The middle diagonal entry is 2: B–A–B and B–C–B. This matrix is a separate three-vertex example.

blocks.title: Match the structure to the task
paragraphs: For a large sparse network, use adjacency lists when neighbor traversal matters. A matrix can be useful when frequent edge lookup matters more than memory.

flashcards.front: What does the degree of a vertex count?
flashcards.back: It counts the edges incident to that vertex.

flashcards.front: Why does the degree sum count each undirected edge twice?
flashcards.back: Each edge has two endpoints. It contributes one to the degree of each endpoint.

flashcards.front: Why does an adjacency list suit a sparse graph?
flashcards.back: It stores existing neighbors. It avoids reserving a cell for every possible pair of vertices.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph has six edges. What is the sum of all vertex degrees?

options.feedback: This counts each edge once. An edge contributes to two endpoint degrees.
Each of the six edges contributes two to the degree sum.
This resembles a square-size calculation. The degree sum depends on edges, not matrix cells.
This divides the edge count by two. Each edge contributes two endpoints, so multiply by two.

questions.prompt: A network has many vertices and few edges. You mainly traverse neighbors. Which representation fits this task?

options.text: An adjacency list
options.feedback: It stores existing connections and gives direct access to each neighbor list.

options.text: An adjacency matrix for its smaller memory use
options.feedback: A matrix uses \(O(|V|^2)\) memory, including absent edges.

options.text: A matrix because every graph is dense
options.feedback: The prompt describes a sparse graph. Density is a property of this graph, not all graphs.

options.text: An edge list because it finds every vertex’s neighbors without scanning
options.feedback: An ordinary edge list may require scanning all edges to find one vertex’s neighbors. An adjacency list stores those neighbors together.

questions.explanation: The task favors neighbor traversal and compact storage of existing edges.

units.label: Topic 02
units.title: Follow the frontier
units.summary: Use a queue to explore a graph in layers. See why the order gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

objectives.text: Trace a FIFO frontier without duplicate discoveries.
Explain the shortest-path guarantee and its assumptions.

blocks.title: Explore one layer at a time
paragraphs: Breadth-first search keeps the next vertices in a queue. The first vertex added is the first vertex removed. This is FIFO order.
Mark a vertex as seen when you enqueue it. Each vertex enters the queue at most once.

blocks.title: Watch the frontier move
blocks.description: Undirected graph: A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E, D–F and E–F. The highlighted vertex \(i\)s being expanded. The caption and seen list describe each step.

frames.caption: Start with A. Mark A as seen and put it in the queue.
Expand A. Discover B and C, in alphabetical order.
Expand B. Discover D. C stays at the front of the queue.
Expand C. Discover E after D.
Expand D. Discover F at distance three.
Expand E. F is already seen, so do not enqueue it again.
Expand F. Its neighbors are already seen.
The queue is empty. Every reachable vertex \(i\)s discovered.

blocks.title: Keep discovery separate from processing
blocks.explanation: Store neighbors in alphabetical order to reproduce the trace. Mark a vertex seen when you enqueue it. This prevents repeated discovery through another edge. The example assumes an adjacency list and a valid start vertex.

blocks.title: Distance grows by one edge
blocks.plain: When \(u\) first discovers \(v\), the distance to \(v\) is the distance to \(u\) plus one.

symbols.meaning: The vertex being expanded.
A neighbor that was not seen before.
The shortest number of edges from the start to \(x\).

blocks.conditions: Here \(d\) counts edges. For equal positive weights, minimum edge count also minimizes total cost. In this diagram, \(d(F)=3\).

blocks.title: Choose the search order
rows: Minimum edge count; also minimum cost for equal positive weights.
Minimum total weight for nonnegative edges.
blocks.caption: The frontier determines what “next” means.

blocks.title: Account for the work
paragraphs: An adjacency list lets the search expand each vertex once and inspect each adjacency entry. The total time is \(O(|V|+|E|)\).
Try the trace again without looking at the next caption. Predict the queue before each step.

flashcards.front: When should BFS mark a vertex as seen?
flashcards.back: When the vertex \(i\)s enqueued. This prevents several neighbors from adding it again.

flashcards.front: When does BFS guarantee a shortest path?
flashcards.back: BFS minimizes edge count. It also minimizes total cost when all edges have equal positive weight. With arbitrary weights, BFS does not guarantee minimum cost.
Each vertex \(i\)s expanded at most once. The algorithm inspects each adjacency entry a bounded number of times.

questions.prompt: Start at A and inspect neighbors alphabetically. After expanding B, which queue remains?

options.text: C, D
options.feedback: A added B and C. Removing B leaves C, then B adds D.

options.text: D, C
options.feedback: This puts a newly discovered vertex before the older frontier entry. A FIFO queue does not do that.

options.text: C, A, D
options.feedback: A is already seen. It must not be enqueued again.

options.text: B, C, D
options.feedback: B has already been removed for expansion. The queue contains waiting vertices, not the vertex currently being expanded.

questions.explanation: The oldest waiting vertex remains first. New vertices join the back.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, how many edges are on a shortest path from A to F?

options.feedback: F has no neighbor directly adjacent to A. Two edges are not enough.
A–B–D–F and A–C–E–F each use three edges.
A longer traversal can use five edges. BFS reaches F after three layers.
A shortest route contains four vertices but only three edges. Distance here counts edges.

questions.explanation: The frontier layers are A; B and C; D and E; then F.

questions.prompt: With adjacency lists, why is BFS \(O(|V|+|E|)\) rather than \(O(|V|\,|E|)\)?

options.text: Each vertex causes a full scan of every graph edge
options.feedback: BFS scans the current vertex’s adjacency list, not all edges for each vertex.

options.text: Vertices are expanded once, and adjacency entries are inspected a bounded number of times
options.feedback: The vertex work and adjacency work add. They are not multiplied.

options.text: The queue automatically removes all edge processing
options.feedback: The queue determines order. The algorithm still inspects neighbors.

options.text: Every discovered neighbor starts another full traversal from A
options.feedback: BFS marks a neighbor on discovery and adds it once. Restarting from A would repeat work that ordinary BFS avoids.

questions.explanation: Add the vertex work and edge work: \(O(|V|)+O(|E|)=O(|V|+|E|)\).

units.label: Topic 03
units.title: Go deep, then return
units.summary: Follow a branch, keep the return path, and understand why depth-first order is different from shortest-path order.

objectives.text: Explain backtracking and the purpose of seen markers.
Give a counterexample to a shortest-path claim for DFS.

blocks.title: Keep a route back
paragraphs: Depth-first search follows an unseen neighbor before it continues with other branches. Recursion stores where to return. An explicit stack can store the same pending work.
When a branch has no unseen neighbor, return to an earlier vertex and inspect its remaining neighbors. This return is backtracking.

blocks.title: Two orders, two behaviors
rows: A stack or recursive return path.
Work from the current deepest branch.
Fewest edges in an unweighted graph.
blocks.caption: Both methods need seen markers for graph traversal.

blocks.title: A direct edge can be discovered late
paragraphs: Use the graph from Topic 02. An alphabetical recursive DFS can discover C along A–B–D–F–E–C. That tree path has five edges.
The graph also contains the direct edge A–C. It has one edge. The first DFS discovery path is therefore not necessarily shortest.

blocks.title: The same broad work bound
blocks.plain: With adjacency lists, DFS runs in time proportional to vertices plus edges.

symbols.meaning: The set of vertices.
The set of edges.
An asymptotic upper bound, not an exact operation count.

blocks.conditions: Mark seen vertices to avoid repeated traversal through cycles.

flashcards.front: What does backtracking do in DFS?
flashcards.back: It returns to earlier pending work after the current branch has no unseen neighbor.

flashcards.front: Why does graph DFS need seen markers?
flashcards.back: A cycle can lead back to an earlier vertex. A seen marker prevents repeated traversal.

flashcards.front: How can DFS miss a shorter path?
flashcards.back: It can discover a vertex through a long branch before it examines a direct or shorter connection.

questions.prompt: A DFS neighbor is already seen. What should ordinary traversal do?

options.text: Skip revisiting it and continue the remaining search
options.feedback: This avoids repeating work through a cycle.

options.text: Remove its seen marker before entering it again
options.feedback: Removing the marker can reintroduce repeated traversal.

options.text: Restart the whole traversal from that vertex
options.feedback: Restarting is not ordinary DFS and can repeat the same cycle.

options.text: Stop the entire search as soon as a seen neighbor appears
options.feedback: An undirected edge leads back to a seen parent. Stop revisiting that neighbor, but continue exploring pending branches.

questions.explanation: The return path preserves pending work. Seen markers prevent visiting the same vertex again.

questions.prompt: DFS discovers C via A–B–D–F–E–C, but edge A–C exists. What follows?

options.text: The DFS tree path is not a shortest path to C
options.feedback: It has five edges, while the direct connection has one.

options.text: DFS always finds a shortest path after backtracking
options.feedback: Backtracking does not change the first-discovery tree into a shortest-path tree.

options.text: The direct edge cannot belong to an undirected graph
options.feedback: An undirected graph can contain the direct edge and the longer route.

options.text: Every path from A to C must therefore contain five edges
options.feedback: The first DFS tree path describes one route. The direct A–C edge is a counterexample to that claim.

questions.explanation: A single counterexample disproves the claim that DFS always gives shortest paths.

units.label: Topic 04
units.title: Find the cheapest route
units.summary: A short route need not be a cheap route. Add weights and track the best known cost.

objectives.text: Compare edge count with total path cost.

blocks.title: Count cost, not just edges
paragraphs: BFS gives the fewest edges in an unweighted graph. A weighted network asks a different question: which route has the smallest total cost?
Use nonnegative edge weights. Start with distance 0 at S and infinity elsewhere. Settle the smallest tentative distance, then try its outgoing edges.

blocks.title: The algorithm as a process
blocks.description: A process diagram: begin with tentative distances, settle the minimum, then relax outgoing edges. Repeat selection and relaxation until the target is settled.

frames.caption: Initialize S at zero and other distances at infinity.
Settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance.
Try outgoing edges and improve any distance that gets cheaper. Repeat selection and relaxation.

blocks.title: Add the cost along a path
blocks.plain: The cost of a path is the sum of its edge weights.

symbols.meaning: A path with vertices v₀ through vₘ.
The number of edges on that path.
The cost of the edge from \(u\) to \(v\).

blocks.conditions: Compare costs in the same units. In this example every edge weight is nonnegative.

blocks.title: Settle the best distance
blocks.description: Directed weighted network. Edge labels are costs. Advance the steps to settle S, A, B and T.

frames.caption: Settle S. Tentative distances become \(d(A)=2\) and \(d(B)=5\).
Settle A at 2. Improve B to 3 and discover T at 8.
Settle B at 3. Improve T to 5 through B.
Settle T at 5. The cheapest route is S–A–B–T.

blocks.title: Keep the better distance
blocks.plain: Replace the tentative distance only if the route through u is cheaper.

symbols.meaning: The best distance to \(v\) found so far.
The vertex currently being expanded.
The cost of its outgoing edge to \(v\).

blocks.conditions: With \(d(A)=2\), \(d(B)=5\) and \(w(A,B)=1\), the new distance to B is min(5, 2+1)=3. Dijkstra’s settling rule requires nonnegative weights.

blocks.title: Compare the routes
blocks.caption: More edges can still mean less cost.

blocks.title: Remember the distinction
points: BFS minimizes the number of edges.
A weighted path adds its edge costs.
Relaxation improves a tentative distance; it does not make an arbitrary distance final.

flashcards.front: Does the path with the fewest edges always have the lowest total weight?
flashcards.back: No. Add the weights. A longer path can have a lower total cost.
When \(d(u)\)+\(w(u,v)\) is smaller than the current \(d(v)\).

questions.prompt: Which route in this network has the lowest total cost from S to T?

options.text: S → A → B → T, cost 3
options.feedback: Three is the number of edges. It is not their total weight.

options.text: S → A → T, cost 8
options.feedback: This uses fewer edges, but 2+6 is larger than 5.

options.text: S → B → T, cost 7
options.feedback: This costs 5+2=7. Going through A improves the route to B.

options.text: S → A → B → T, cost 5
options.feedback: Its three weights sum to 2+1+2=5.

questions.explanation: Compare the sums. The three-edge route costs 5, less than either two-edge route.

questions.prompt: The current \(d(B)\) is 5. With \(d(A)=2\) and \(w(A,B)=1\), what does relaxing A → B do?

options.text: Keep \(d(B)=5\) because B was discovered earlier
options.feedback: Discovery does not settle B. A cheaper candidate may replace its tentative distance.

options.text: Set \(d(B)=3\) because 2+1 is smaller than 5
options.feedback: The candidate through A costs 3, so it improves the tentative distance.

options.text: Set \(d(B)=1\) because that is the last edge weight
options.feedback: The last edge is only part of the route. Include the cost to reach A.

options.text: Set \(d(B)=8\) by adding the old distance to the candidate
options.feedback: Relaxation compares the old and candidate distances; it does not add them.

questions.explanation: Take min(5,2+1)=3. The candidate uses the full cost from S through A to B.

units.label: Topic 05
units.title: Update a probability
units.summary: Use evidence and base rates together. Then count successes in independent repeated trials.

objectives.text: Compute a conditional probability from counts.
Use a binomial model only when its assumptions hold.

blocks.title: Begin with a concrete population
paragraphs: An alert catches 80% of urgent messages. That does not mean 80% of alerts are urgent. The answer also depends on how common urgent messages are.
Use 1,000 messages. Of these, 200 are urgent. The alert catches 160 urgent messages and also flags 80 of the 800 other messages.

blocks.title: Reverse the condition carefully
blocks.plain: Two thirds of the flagged messages are urgent. The denominator includes both true and false alerts.

symbols.meaning: The message is urgent.
The alert flags the message.
The message is not urgent.
The base rate of urgent messages: 0.2.

blocks.conditions: The evidence must have positive probability. Here \(P(E)=0.24\), and the stated rates apply to this population.

blocks.title: Repeat a trial under the same conditions
paragraphs: A fair coin gives success probability 1/2 on each independent toss. In three tosses, there are three positions for exactly one head.
Count the arrangements, then multiply by the probability of each arrangement. This gives the binomial formula.

blocks.title: Count exactly \(k\) successes
blocks.plain: The binomial probability combines the number of arrangements with their probability. The expected success count is \(n\) times \(p\).

symbols.meaning: The fixed number of trials.
The same success probability on each trial.
The number of successful trials.
An integer from 0 through \(n\).
The average success count over repeated experiments.

blocks.conditions: The trials are independent, with identical success probability. For three fair tosses, the expected number of heads is 1.5; one experiment still has an integer count.

blocks.title: Read the three-toss distribution
blocks.caption: The probabilities sum to 1. Symmetry gives the same probability for one and two heads.

blocks.title: Keep the assumptions visible
points: \(P(H\mid E)\) and \(P(E\mid H)\) use different reference populations.
Include false alerts and the base rate when conditioning on an alert.
A binomial model needs independent trials with the same success probability.

flashcards.back: Not generally. They condition on different populations. Use the base rate and false-alert rate to reverse the condition.

flashcards.front: There are 160 urgent alerts among 240 alerts. Which fraction gives \(P(\mathrm{urgent}\mid\mathrm{alert})\)?
Which assumptions make a fixed success count binomial?
flashcards.back: A fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability.

questions.prompt: The alert flags 160 urgent and 80 nonurgent messages. What fraction of flagged messages are urgent?

options.feedback: There are 240 flagged messages, so the fraction is 160/240.
That is the sensitivity: 160 of 200 urgent messages are flagged. The question conditions on alerts.
That is the population base rate. The alert supplies additional evidence.
That is 160/1000, the joint population fraction. Restrict the denominator to flagged messages.

questions.explanation: Condition on the alert: keep only flagged messages. Of the 240 that remain, 160 are urgent.

questions.prompt: Three independent fair coin tosses are made. What is the probability of exactly two heads?

options.feedback: That is the probability of a head on one toss, not of two heads across three tosses.
That overcounts the outcomes with exactly two heads. Only three of the eight equally likely sequences qualify.
HHT, HTH and THH are three distinct sequences, each with probability 1/8.
One specific sequence has probability 1/8. There are three sequences with exactly two heads.

questions.explanation: Choose two positions from three: 3 arrangements. Each has probability (1/2)³, giving 3/8.
